In [[probability theory]], a [[random variable]] <math>Y</math> is said to be '''mean independent''' of random variable <math>X</math> [[if and only if]] its [[conditional mean]] <math>E(Y \mid X = x)</math> equals its (unconditional) [[expected value|mean]] <math>E(Y)</math> for all <math>x</math> such that the probability density/mass of <math>X</math> at <math>x</math>, <math>f_X(x)</math>, is not zero. Otherwise, <math>Y</math> is said to be '''mean dependent''' on <math>X</math>.

[[independence (probability theory)|Stochastic independence]] implies mean independence, but the converse is not true.;<ref>{{Harvtxt|Cameron|Trivedi|2009|p=23}}</ref><ref name=":0">{{Harvtxt|Wooldridge|2010|pp=54, 907}}</ref> moreover, mean independence implies uncorrelatedness while the converse is not true. Unlike stochastic independence and uncorrelatedness, mean independence is not symmetric: it is possible for <math>Y</math> to be mean-independent of <math>X</math> even though <math>X</math> is mean-dependent on <math>Y</math>.

The concept of mean independence is often used in [[econometrics]]<ref name=":0" /> to have a middle ground between the strong assumption of independent random variables (<math>X_1 \perp X_2</math>) and the weak assumption of uncorrelated random variables <math>(\operatorname{Cov}(X_1, X_2) = 0).</math>
